subsystems.name: Substrate
subsystems.role: provides mechanical support and forms the main body that breaks down after use.

subsystems.name: Conductors
subsystems.role: carry current between components and dissolve or degrade harmlessly.

subsystems.name: Semiconductors
subsystems.role: switch and amplify signals, the active core of any circuit.

subsystems.name: Dielectrics and encapsulation
subsystems.role: insulate components and set the timeline over which the device degrades.

subsystems.name: Power sources
subsystems.role: supply energy for the device's working life without leaving persistent waste.

subsystems.name: Interconnects and packaging
subsystems.role: join components and protect them until end of life, then release them to the environment.

buildSteps.title: Design for a target lifetime
buildSteps.detail: Choose materials whose dissolution or biodegradation rate matches the intended use — days for a skin patch, months for a soil sensor.

buildSteps.title: Form the substrate
buildSteps.detail: Cast or spin a thin film of cellulose, silk or a biodegradable polymer to act as the flexible base.

buildSteps.title: Deposit and pattern conductors
buildSteps.detail: Evaporate or print biodegradable metals such as magnesium or zinc, then etch or print them into circuit traces.

buildSteps.title: Add semiconductors and dielectrics
buildSteps.detail: Deposit organic semiconductors or transfer-print silicon nanomembranes, then layer biodegradable insulators on top.

buildSteps.title: Integrate the power source
buildSteps.detail: Print or attach a biodegradable battery or supercapacitor, or add an antenna for wireless power.

buildSteps.title: Encapsulate for controlled degradation
buildSteps.detail: Apply a biodegradable coating whose thickness and chemistry decide when the device starts to break down.

buildSteps.title: Test performance and degradation
buildSteps.detail: Measure electrical behaviour while the device operates, and track its breakdown in compost, water or body fluid.

buildSteps.title: Dispose or implant
buildSteps.detail: At end of life the device is composted, flushed or left in the body, where it degrades into harmless compounds.

prerequisites.why: magnesium and zinc work but corrode quickly; conductive polymers are less stable than copper.
organic and nanomembrane options exist in labs but lag far behind silicon in speed and reliability.
a device must work reliably for its intended life and then vanish on cue, which is hard to guarantee.
most demonstrations are made one at a time in clean rooms; printing and roll-to-roll lines are not yet established.
degradation products must be non-toxic, especially for implantable or skin-mounted devices.

pathway.milestone: lab demonstrations of transient sensors, implants and simple circuits that dissolve in water or biofluids
pathway.unlocks: proof that electronics can be built from materials that disappear.

pathway.milestone: pilot production of simple biodegradable devices such as environmental sensors and disposable RFID tags
pathway.unlocks: real-world testing of reliability and degradation outside the lab.

pathway.milestone: integration into consumer products with a defined short life, such as wearable patches and smart packaging
pathway.unlocks: a route to cut e-waste where devices are discarded quickly.

pathway.milestone: complex biodegradable electronics with onboard power, sensing and communication for medical and agricultural use
pathway.unlocks: devices that monitor and then safely disappear, avoiding a second removal procedure or collection step.
